JavaScript: Core Language & Execution

7 questions
Q1

Hoisting for var, let, const and function declarations

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

The engine processes code in two phases. In the creation phase, it scans the scope and registers every declaration. In the execution phase, it runs the code line by line. Hoisting is the result of the first phase: names exist before their line runs. The code does not physically move.

Declaration Registered? Initial value Access before the line
var x Yes, in function scope undefined Gives undefined
let x / const x Yes, in block scope Not initialized ReferenceError (TDZ)
function f() {} Yes, with the full body The function Call works
const f = () => {} As const Not initialized ReferenceError
var f = function () {} As var undefined TypeError: f is not a function
class C {} Like let Not initialized ReferenceError

Priority rule: if a function declaration and a var have the same name, the function wins during creation. The var assignment then overwrites it when its line runs.

Traps:

  • "let and const are not hoisted" is wrong. They are hoisted, but not initialized. Proof: an inner let x shadows an outer x from the first line of the block, and the access throws.
  • Function declarations inside blocks (if (...) { function f() {} }) behave differently in sloppy and strict mode. Do not write them. Use a const function expression.

Follow-up: "Why does var hoisting cause bugs?" Answer: a read before assignment gives a silent undefined instead of an error, and var ignores block scope, so a variable in an if or a for leaks to the whole function.

Q2

Temporal dead zone (TDZ)

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

The TDZ is the time between the start of a scope and the line that initializes a let, const or class. In this time, the name exists but has no value. Any access throws ReferenceError.

The TDZ is about time, not position in the text:

A parameter default can also hit the TDZ:

Why the TDZ exists:

  1. It turns use-before-define bugs into errors. With var, the same bug gives a silent undefined.
  2. It makes const reliable. A const must have exactly one value for its whole life. Without the TDZ, code could see it as undefined first, then as its real value.
  3. It gives a defined behavior for class declarations and future features such as guards.

Follow-up: "Is typeof always safe?" Answer: it is safe for undeclared names (gives 'undefined'). It throws for a let/const in its TDZ.

Q3

How the execution context works

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

An execution context is the record that the engine creates to run a piece of code. Types: global, function and eval. Each context holds:

  • A lexical environment: an environment record (the variables and functions of this scope) plus a reference to the outer environment.
  • A variable environment: where var declarations live (historically separate, today mostly an implementation detail).
  • The this binding.

Life of a function call:

  1. Creation phase: create the environment record, register parameters, function declarations, var (set to undefined), let/const (uninitialized). Set this. Set the outer reference to the scope where the function was written (lexical).
  2. Execution phase: run the code, assign values, call other functions.
  3. When the function returns, the engine pops its context from the call stack. The environment stays in memory only if a closure still references it.

Follow-up: "What is a stack overflow?" Answer: each call adds a context to the stack. Recursion with no base case adds contexts until the engine hits its limit and throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded.

Q4

Call stack vs task queue vs microtask queue

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

JavaScript runs on one main thread. These three structures decide what runs next.

Structure Contains Order When it runs
Call stack Execution contexts of the code running now LIFO Immediately
Microtask queue Promise.then/catch/finally, await continuations, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver FIFO When the stack is empty. The engine drains all of it, including microtasks added during the drain.
Task (macrotask) queue setTimeout, setInterval, I/O callbacks, UI events, MessageChannel, setImmediate (Node) FIFO per source One task per event loop turn

One turn of the event loop in a browser:

  1. Take the oldest task and run it until the stack is empty.
  2. Run all microtasks.
  3. If it is time, render: requestAnimationFrame callbacks, style, layout, paint.
  4. Repeat.

Node differences: the loop has phases (timers → pending callbacks → poll for I/O → check for setImmediate → close). process.nextTick callbacks run before Promise microtasks.

Follow-up: "Is setTimeout(fn, 0) immediate?" Answer: no. It schedules a task after at least 0 ms. It runs after the current script and all microtasks. Browsers clamp nested timers to at least 4 ms after five levels.

Q5

How the event loop prioritizes Promises over setTimeout

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

The main script is itself a task. When it finishes, the stack is empty, so the engine drains the microtask queue before it takes the next task. Promise callbacks are microtasks. setTimeout callbacks are tasks. So all ready Promise callbacks run first.

Actual order: 1, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 4.5, 5, 6. The microtasks run in the order they were queued. promise 2 is queued only when promise 1 finishes, so it runs after the other first-level microtasks.

Starvation risk:

The same code with setTimeout(loop) does not freeze the page, because each call is a separate task and the browser can render between tasks.

Follow-up: "Where does await resume?" Answer: in a microtask, after the awaited promise settles.

Q6

Lexical scoping with an example

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Lexical (static) scoping means the place where you write a function decides which variables it can see. The engine fixes this when it parses the code. The call site does not matter.

In a dynamically scoped language, the result would be 'local to run', because the lookup would follow the call chain. JavaScript does not do this for variables.

Scope chain: a lookup starts in the current scope and goes outward, one level at a time, to the global scope. It never goes inward.

Scope levels: global, module, function, and block (let, const, class only).

The exception is this. In a normal function, this depends on how you call the function (dynamic). Arrow functions take this lexically.

Follow-up: "How does lexical scope relate to closures?" Answer: lexical scope is the rule. A closure is a function that keeps its lexical environment after the outer function returns (Q8).

Q7

Undeclared variable vs undefined

Answer it out loud first. Then check.
Case Example Read result typeof
Declared, no value let a; undefined 'undefined'
Declared, set to undefined let b = undefined; undefined 'undefined'
Undeclared (no declaration) ReferenceError: c is not defined 'undefined' (no error)
In TDZ let d later in block ReferenceError: Cannot access 'd' before initialization Throws
Missing property obj.missing undefined (no error) 'undefined'

Assignment to an undeclared name:

ES modules and class bodies are always strict. In old scripts, add 'use strict'.

undefined vs null: undefined means "no value was assigned." null is a value you assign to say "empty on purpose." null == undefined is true, null === undefined is false.

Follow-up: "How do you safely check whether a global exists?" Answer: typeof someGlobal !== 'undefined', or 'someGlobal' in globalThis.

Functions & Closures

6 questions
Q8

Closure, and when it causes memory leaks

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

A closure is a function together with a reference to the lexical environment where it was created. The function can read and change those variables after the outer function has returned. Every function in JavaScript is a closure. The term matters when the function outlives its outer scope.

Real uses:

  • Private state (module pattern, factories).
  • Callbacks and event handlers that need data from their setup.
  • Function factories: const add5 = makeAdder(5).
  • Memoization caches, debounce, once.

The classic loop question:

With var, the three closures share one i. With let, each iteration creates a new binding.

When closures leak memory: a closure keeps its whole environment reachable for as long as the closure itself is reachable. A leak happens when a long-lived object holds a closure that holds large data:

Common causes: listeners never removed, setInterval never cleared, callbacks pushed into a global array or cache, closures stored on DOM nodes that are later detached.

V8 detail: all closures created in the same scope share one context object. If any one of them uses bigData, all of them keep it alive, even closures that never mention it.

Fixes:

Also: clearInterval, set large references to null when done, use WeakMap / WeakRef for caches keyed by objects. In React, return a cleanup function from useEffect.

Follow-up: "How do you find the leak?" Answer: DevTools → Memory → heap snapshot before and after the action, compare, and look at the retainers of the objects that grow.

Q9

Function declaration vs function expression

Answer it out loud first. Then check.
Declaration Expression
Hoisting Name and body. Callable before the line. Follows its variable: var → undefined, let/const → TDZ
Name Required Optional. A named expression's name is visible only inside its own body (useful for recursion and stack traces).
Where Statement position Any expression position: argument, return value, object property, IIFE
Conditional creation Unreliable inside blocks Works: const fn = cond ? a : b
Reassign Possible but confusing With const, impossible

IIFE (immediately invoked function expression), common in older code to create a private scope:

Arrow functions are expressions with extra differences: no own this, arguments, super or new.target. They cannot be constructors.

Which to use: declarations for top-level named helpers (readable, hoisted). const + arrow for callbacks and small functions. Teams often pick one style. Be consistent.

Follow-up: "Why might a team ban declarations?" Answer: hoisting lets code call functions before their definition, which some teams consider hard to read. A const forces define-before-use.

Q10

How this behaves

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

For a normal function, this is set at call time by how you call it. Four rules, from highest priority to lowest:

Rule Call form this
new binding new Fn() The new object
Explicit binding fn.call(obj), fn.apply(obj), fn.bind(obj)() obj
Implicit binding obj.fn() obj (the object before the dot)
Default binding fn() undefined in strict mode, globalThis in sloppy mode

Lost this — the most common bug:

Arrow functions: no own this. They use this from the surrounding scope at creation time. call, apply and bind cannot change it.

Do not use an arrow function as an object method that needs this:

Event handlers:

e.target is the element that was clicked (can be a child). e.currentTarget is the element with the listener.

In classes: methods lose this when passed as callbacks. Fix with an arrow class field (handle = () => {...}) or bind in the constructor.

Follow-up: "What does bind + new do?" Answer: new wins. The bound this is ignored, but bound arguments still apply.

Q11

bind, call and apply with use cases

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

All three set this explicitly.

Use cases:

  1. Fix this for callbacks: el.addEventListener('click', this.onClick.bind(this)).
  2. Partial application: const log = console.log.bind(console, '[api]'); log('started');.
  3. Borrow methods from another type: Array.prototype.map.call('abc', (ch) => ch.toUpperCase()) → ['A','B','C'].
  4. Spread arrays into arguments (old style): Math.max.apply(null, nums). Today: Math.max(...nums).
  5. Call a parent constructor in old prototype code: Animal.call(this, name).

Rules:

  • A bound function cannot be bound again to another this. The first bind wins.
  • Arrow functions ignore the this argument of all three.
  • bind creates a new function each time. el.removeEventListener('click', this.fn.bind(this)) does not remove anything. Store the bound function and reuse it.

Interview task — implement bind:

This simple version does not handle new. Say that, and mention that the full version checks new.target.

Q12

Currying and why it is useful

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Currying transforms a function with N arguments into a chain of N functions with one argument each: f(a, b, c) becomes f(a)(b)(c).

Currying vs partial application: currying always produces unary steps. Partial application fixes some arguments and returns a function for the rest (bind does this). In practice, people often use the word currying for both.

Why it is useful:

  • Configure once, use many times:
  • Curried functions fit composition and point-free style (Q13), because each step takes one input.
  • Event handlers with data: onClick={handleSelect(item.id)} where handleSelect = (id) => (e) => ....

Limits: fn.length ignores default and rest parameters, so generic curry breaks on them. Deep currying hurts readability and stack traces. Use it where it removes repetition, not everywhere.

Q13

Function composition

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Composition builds a new function from smaller ones. The output of one becomes the input of the next. Math notation: (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)).

pipe reads in execution order, so most teams prefer it.

Async version:

Why it matters:

  • Small, pure, single-purpose functions are easy to test.
  • You build behavior by combining parts instead of by writing large functions.
  • Middleware (Express, Redux) uses the same idea: a chain of functions that each transform or pass along.

Requirement: each function in the chain takes one argument. Use currying (Q12) to fit multi-argument functions.

Follow-up: "What is the identity of compose?" Answer: x => x. pipe() with no functions returns the input unchanged, because reduce starts from x.

Objects & Prototypes

5 questions
Q14

Prototype chaining

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Every object has a hidden internal slot [[Prototype]] that points to another object or to null. When you read a property that the object does not have, the engine follows this link and searches the next object. The linked objects form the prototype chain.

Built-in chains:

Three names that people confuse:

Name What it is
[[Prototype]] The internal link that every object has
obj.__proto__ Old accessor for that link. Deprecated. Use Object.getPrototypeOf(obj) / Object.setPrototypeOf.
Fn.prototype A normal property on functions. It becomes the [[Prototype]] of objects made with new Fn().

Why it matters: methods live once on the prototype, not on each instance. This saves memory. Changing a prototype affects all objects that inherit from it, so never modify built-in prototypes like Array.prototype in application code.

Performance: a long chain makes lookups of missing properties slower, and Object.setPrototypeOf on an existing object deoptimizes it. Set the prototype at creation.

Follow-up: "How does instanceof work?" Answer: a instanceof B walks the chain of a and checks whether any link equals B.prototype.

Q15

Object.create() vs class-based inheritance

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Both produce the same structure: objects linked through [[Prototype]]. They differ in syntax and features.

Object.create class
Mechanism Sets [[Prototype]] directly Constructor + prototype, linked with extends
Initialization Manual (init method or properties) constructor, super()
Privacy Closures only #private fields and methods
Static members Manual static
Strict mode Depends on file Always
Call without new Not applicable TypeError
Hoisting Not applicable TDZ like let
No-prototype object Object.create(null) Not possible directly

Object.create(null) creates an object with no inherited properties. Use it for dictionaries where keys come from users, so a key like toString or __proto__ cannot collide with inherited members. Map is often a better choice.

When to use which: class for application code and libraries (readable, tooling support, TypeScript friendly). Object.create for small delegation cases, prototype-free maps, and to explain how JavaScript inheritance really works.

Follow-up: "Is JavaScript class-based?" Answer: no. class is syntax over prototypes. There is no copy of a class into an instance. Lookups delegate along the chain at runtime.

Q16

How property lookup works

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Read obj.prop:

  1. If obj has an own property prop: return its value, or call its getter.
  2. Else: move to Object.getPrototypeOf(obj) and repeat.
  3. At null: return undefined. A missing property does not throw. A read on undefined or null itself does throw (TypeError).

Write obj.prop = value (more complex):

Situation Result
Own writable property exists Value changes
Own property is non-writable Fails: silent in sloppy mode, TypeError in strict
A setter exists on the chain The setter runs with this = obj. No own property is created.
A non-writable data property exists on the chain Fails. No own property is created.
Not found, or a writable data property on the chain A new own property is created on obj. It shadows the inherited one.

Checking properties:

Iteration differences: for...in includes inherited enumerable properties. Object.keys, Object.entries and spread include only own enumerable string keys.

Follow-up: "Why prefer Object.hasOwn to obj.hasOwnProperty?" Answer: an object from Object.create(null) has no hasOwnProperty method, and an object can override it. Object.hasOwn always works.

Q17

Shallow copy vs deep copy

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Shallow copy: a new top-level object. Nested objects and arrays are still shared references.

Deep copy: a new object at every level. No shared references.

Shallow tools: { ...obj }, Object.assign({}, obj), [...arr], arr.slice(), Array.from(arr).

Deep tools compared:

Method Handles Does not handle
structuredClone (built in, browsers and Node 17+) Date, Map, Set, RegExp, ArrayBuffer, typed arrays, cycles Functions, DOM nodes, class prototypes (result is a plain object), getters (copied as values), symbols as keys
JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) Plain data only Drops undefined and functions; Date → string; Map/Set → {}; NaN/Infinity → null; throws on cycles and BigInt
lodash.cloneDeep Most types, keeps prototypes Extra dependency
Manual recursion What you code Easy to get wrong (cycles, special types)

Interview task — simple deep clone with cycle support:

When it matters: state updates in React/Redux (you usually need only a shallow copy of the changed path, not a full deep clone), caching, undo history, passing data to code that may mutate it.

Follow-up: "Is a full deep clone for every state update good?" Answer: no. It is slow and breaks reference equality for unchanged parts, which causes extra re-renders. Copy only the changed path (or use Immer).

Q18

Object.freeze() vs Object.seal()

Answer it out loud first. Then check.
Ability Normal preventExtensions seal freeze
Add new properties Yes No No No
Delete properties Yes Yes No No
Change values Yes Yes Yes No
Reconfigure (getter, enumerable) Yes Yes No No
Check — Object.isExtensible Object.isSealed Object.isFrozen

In sloppy mode, the blocked operations fail silently. This hides bugs. Use strict mode (modules are strict).

Deep freeze:

Uses: constants and configuration objects, enum-like objects, defensive protection in development (Redux Toolkit and Immer freeze state in dev mode to catch accidental mutation).

Limits: freeze does not protect the internal data of Map, Set or Date (frozenMap.set() still works), and frozen objects can be slower to create in hot paths. const is a different thing: it blocks reassignment of the variable, not changes to the object.

Follow-up: "How does TypeScript readonly compare?" Answer: readonly is compile-time only. Object.freeze is enforced at runtime. Object.freeze also returns a Readonly<T> type in TypeScript.

Asynchronous JavaScript

7 questions
Q19

Promise states and chaining

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

A Promise is an object that represents a value that will be available later, or an error.

States:

  • pending: the initial state.
  • fulfilled: the operation succeeded. The promise has a value.
  • rejected: the operation failed. The promise has a reason (usually an Error).

Fulfilled and rejected are both settled. A settled promise never changes state. Extra calls to resolve or reject are ignored.

Note: resolve(otherPromise) does not fulfill with a promise. It locks the promise to follow otherPromise (it is "resolved" but can still be pending).

Chaining rules: each .then, .catch or .finally returns a new promise.

The handler The next promise
Returns a value v Fulfills with v
Returns a promise or thenable Follows it
Throws Rejects with the thrown error
Is missing for this outcome Passes the same value or error through

Common bugs:

  1. Forgetting return inside .then: the next step gets undefined and does not wait.
  2. Nesting .then inside .then instead of returning: callback hell again.
  3. .then(onOk, onErr) does not catch errors thrown by onOk. A trailing .catch does.
  4. A .catch in the middle swallows errors. Rethrow if the chain must stop.

Follow-up: "Is the executor function sync or async?" Answer: sync. new Promise(fn) runs fn immediately. Only the .then callbacks are async (microtasks).

Q20

async/await vs Promises internally

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

async/await is syntax over Promises and generators. It does not add a new concurrency model.

  • An async function always returns a Promise. return x fulfills it with x. throw e rejects it with e.
  • await expr converts expr to a promise (Promise.resolve(expr)), suspends the function and returns control to the caller. When the promise settles, the engine resumes the function in a microtask with the value, or throws the reason at the await line.
  • The engine saves the function's local state between suspensions, like a generator. Before native support, transpilers turned async functions into generators plus a runner.

Practical differences:

Promises (.then) async/await
Readability Chain Looks like sync code
Error handling .catch try/catch (also catches sync errors in the same block)
Branches and loops Awkward Natural if, for, while
Debugging Callbacks in stack Better async stack traces in V8
Parallel work Promise.all Still Promise.all — await alone is sequential

The sequential trap:

Performance note: modern V8 needs fewer microtask ticks for await on a native promise than older versions. Do not rely on exact tick counts in code.

Follow-up: "Can you use await at the top level?" Answer: yes, in ES modules (top-level await). Not in CommonJS or classic scripts.

Q21

What happens if you don't await an async function

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

The function starts running synchronously until its first await. Then it returns a pending promise, and the caller continues at once.

Consequences:

  1. You get a Promise, not the value. const n = getCount(); n + 1 gives '[object Promise]1'.
  2. Race conditions: later code runs before the work finishes. Example: you respond to an HTTP request before the database write completes, and the write fails silently.
  3. Errors escape try/catch:
  1. Unhandled rejections: Node 15+ crashes the process by default (--unhandled-rejections=throw). Browsers log an error and fire unhandledrejection.
  2. In loops, arr.forEach(async (x) => await f(x)) does not wait for anything. forEach ignores returned promises. Use for...of with await (sequential) or Promise.all(arr.map(f)) (parallel).

Intentional fire-and-forget (analytics, non-critical cache warmup) is fine if you handle errors:

Prevention: the lint rules @typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises and no-misused-promises.

Follow-up: "Does an unawaited async function run in parallel?" Answer: it runs concurrently on the same thread. Its synchronous part runs immediately. Real parallelism needs workers.

Q22

Implement Promise.all() manually

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Spec behavior to copy:

  • Accepts any iterable, not only arrays.
  • Non-promise values count as fulfilled.
  • Results keep the input order, not the finish order.
  • Fulfills with [] at once for an empty input.
  • Rejects with the first rejection reason. It does not cancel the others.

Why a counter and not results.length? Results are assigned by index. Setting results[2] first makes length 3 while index 0 and 1 are still empty.

Bonus — allSettled:

Follow-up: "Does Promise.all run the promises in parallel?" Answer: no. Promises are already running when you create them. Promise.all only waits for them. The work runs concurrently because you started it all before waiting.

Q23

Promise.all vs allSettled vs race vs any

Answer it out loud first. Then check.
Method Fulfills Rejects Result shape
Promise.all When all fulfill At the first rejection Array of values
Promise.allSettled When all settle Never Array of { status: 'fulfilled', value } or { status: 'rejected', reason }
Promise.race If the first to settle fulfills If the first to settle rejects One value or one reason
Promise.any At the first fulfillment When all reject One value, or AggregateError with .errors

Empty input: all and allSettled fulfill with []. any rejects with AggregateError. race stays pending forever.

When to use:

Trap with race timeouts: the losing request still runs and uses resources. Cancel it with AbortController:

Follow-up: "What is the difference between race and any?" Answer: race settles with the first result of any kind, including a rejection. any ignores rejections until one promise fulfills.

Q24

Handle concurrent async requests with limits

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Problem: Promise.all(urls.map(fetch)) with 1,000 URLs opens 1,000 requests at once. This can hit rate limits, exhaust sockets or memory, and overload the server.

Solution: a worker pool. Start N workers. Each worker takes the next index until no work remains.

Why not batches?

Batching leaves slots idle. The pool starts a new request as soon as any slot is free.

Error handling choices:

  • Fail fast: the code above. The first error rejects mapWithLimit, but running workers continue. Add a shared stopped flag to stop them.
  • Collect all: wrap the task in try/catch and store { ok: false, error } like allSettled.
  • Retry: wrap the task with retry and exponential backoff for 429/5xx responses.

A reusable limiter (the idea behind p-limit):

Follow-up: "Is nextIndex++ a race condition?" Answer: no. JavaScript runs one piece of code at a time on the thread. A worker can only lose control at an await, and the read and increment happen before it.

Q25

Callback hell and modern solutions

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Callback hell is code where each async step runs inside the callback of the previous step.

The real problems (more important than the indentation):

  1. Repeated error handling at every level. One missed if (err) loses an error.
  2. Inversion of control: you trust third-party code to call your callback exactly once, asynchronously, with the right arguments. It can call it twice, never, or synchronously ("Zalgo").
  3. Sequential and parallel flows are hard to express. Running three calls in parallel and waiting for all needs manual counters.
  4. try/catch does not work across callbacks.

Solutions, in order of history:

  1. Named functions and modules: flatten the pyramid. They do not fix error handling or trust.
  2. Libraries such as async.js (waterfall, parallel).
  3. Promises: settle once (fixes trust), errors propagate to one .catch, Promise.all for parallel.
  4. async/await: linear code with try/catch.
  1. Async iterators and streams (for await...of) for sequences of values over time.

Callbacks are still correct for repeated events (addEventListener, stream.on('data')) and synchronous helpers (map, sort).

Performance & Memory

5 questions
Q26

What causes memory leaks in JavaScript

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

The garbage collector frees only objects that no root can reach. A leak is memory that is still reachable, but that the program no longer needs. The GC cannot know your intent, so it keeps it.

Common causes with examples:

  1. Accidental globals:
  1. Timers that are never cleared:
  1. Event listeners that are never removed (on window, document, sockets, Node EventEmitter). Node warns: MaxListenersExceededWarning: Possible EventEmitter memory leak detected.
  2. Detached DOM nodes:
  1. Closures that capture large data (Q8).
  2. Unbounded caches: a Map or object that only grows.

Fix: an LRU cache with a size limit, a TTL, or a WeakMap keyed by the object so the entry dies with the key.

  1. Pending promises and subscriptions that never settle or unsubscribe (RxJS, WebSocket handlers, store subscriptions).
  2. Logging: console.log(hugeObject) keeps the object alive while DevTools is open.

Server-side (Node) specific: module-level arrays or maps that collect per-request data, request objects stored in closures of long-lived callbacks, and global caches without eviction. Because a server runs for weeks, a small leak per request eventually crashes it with JavaScript heap out of memory.

How to find a leak:

  1. Reproduce: repeat the action (open and close a modal 20 times).
  2. Chrome DevTools → Memory → Heap snapshot before and after. Use the Comparison view, sorted by size delta.
  3. Check the Retainers panel to see which reference keeps the object alive.
  4. Search for "Detached" in the snapshot to find detached DOM trees.
  5. Node: run with --inspect, open chrome://inspect, take snapshots the same way. Watch process.memoryUsage().heapUsed over time.

Follow-up: "What is the difference between Map and WeakMap for caches?" Answer: a Map holds its keys strongly. A WeakMap holds object keys weakly, so when the key object has no other references, the entry can be collected. WeakMap is not iterable and has no size.

Q27

How garbage collection works (mark-and-sweep)

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

JavaScript manages memory automatically. You allocate by creating values. The engine frees memory with a garbage collector.

Mark-and-sweep algorithm:

  1. Roots: the starting points that are always reachable: the global object, local variables and parameters on the current call stack, active closures, and engine handles.
  2. Mark: start at each root and follow every reference. Mark every object you reach.
  3. Sweep: walk the heap and free every unmarked object.
  4. Compact (optional): move live objects together to reduce fragmentation.

Why not reference counting? Reference counting frees an object when its count reaches zero. It fails on cycles:

Old Internet Explorer used reference counting for DOM objects, and cycles between JS and the DOM leaked. Modern engines do not have this problem.

V8 implementation (Orinoco):

  • Generational hypothesis: most objects die young.
  • Young generation (small, about 1–16 MB per semi-space): new objects go here. A minor GC (Scavenger) copies the surviving objects to the other semi-space. It is fast because it touches only live objects.
  • Objects that survive two minor GCs move to the old generation.
  • Old generation: a major GC uses mark-sweep-compact.
  • To keep pauses short, V8 marks incrementally (small steps between JS execution), concurrently (on helper threads while JS runs) and in parallel (several threads during the pause).

Practical consequences:

  • Short-lived temporary objects are cheap.
  • Creating many medium-lived objects (they survive into the old generation) is expensive.
  • You cannot control or force GC in normal code. delete obj.prop or x = null only removes a reference. The memory is freed later, if nothing else refers to it.
  • Node's default heap limit can be raised with --max-old-space-size=4096 (MB). This hides a leak; it does not fix it.

Follow-up: "What are WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry?" Answer: WeakRef holds an object without keeping it alive. FinalizationRegistry runs a callback some time after an object is collected. Both are non-deterministic. Use them only for caches, never for program logic.

Q28

Difference between debounce and throttle

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Both limit how often a function runs when an event fires many times.

Debounce Throttle
Rule Wait until the calls stop for N ms, then run once Run at most once per N ms while calls continue
10 s of continuous events, N = 1 s 1 call (at the end) About 10 calls (regular)
Use Search box suggestions, form autosave, window resize end, validate after typing Scroll position, infinite scroll check, mousemove/drag, game input, rate-limited API

Details the interviewer may ask:

  • Leading vs trailing: a leading debounce runs at the first call and ignores the rest until quiet. The trailing throttle call above makes sure the last position is not lost.
  • Cancel: add debounced.cancel = () => clearTimeout(timer) and call it on unmount.
  • this and arguments: use fn.apply(this, args) so the wrapped function works as a method.
  • In React, create the debounced function once (useMemo or useRef). A new debounced function on each render resets the timer every time and never fires correctly.
  • For visual updates, requestAnimationFrame is often better than throttle: it runs once per frame, synced with rendering.

Follow-up: "Search box: debounce or throttle?" Answer: debounce, about 300 ms, plus cancel or ignore stale responses with AbortController, so an old slow response cannot overwrite a newer one.

Q29

How browsers optimize JavaScript execution

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

V8 (Chrome, Edge, Node) uses a multi-tier pipeline:

  1. Parser: builds an AST. Pre-parsing skips the bodies of functions that are not called yet (lazy parsing), to start faster.
  2. Ignition: compiles to bytecode and interprets it. While it runs, it collects type feedback (which shapes and types each operation sees).
  3. Sparkplug: a fast baseline compiler. It turns bytecode into simple machine code without optimizations.
  4. Maglev: a mid-tier optimizing compiler. Fast to compile, good code.
  5. TurboFan: the top-tier optimizing compiler for hot functions. It uses the type feedback to make speculative assumptions ("x is always a small integer") and inlines functions.

If an assumption fails at runtime, the engine deoptimizes: it drops the optimized code and goes back to bytecode. Repeated deoptimization is expensive.

Hidden classes and inline caches:

Each property access site keeps an inline cache of the shapes it saw:

  • Monomorphic (1 shape): fastest. Direct offset load.
  • Polymorphic (2–4 shapes): still fast.
  • Megamorphic (many shapes): slow, generic lookup.

Code that helps the engine:

  • Create objects with all properties in the constructor, in the same order.
  • Do not add or delete properties on hot objects after creation. Set to null/undefined instead.
  • Keep variables and array elements to one type. [1, 2, 3] (packed small integers) is faster than [1, 'a', {}] or an array with holes.
  • Keep hot functions monomorphic: call them with the same argument types.
  • Avoid arguments tricks, eval and with in hot code.

Browser-level performance usually matters more than JIT details:

  • Load: smaller bundles, code splitting, defer/async scripts, compression, HTTP caching.
  • Rendering: avoid layout thrashing (reading offsetHeight after writing styles in a loop forces a synchronous layout). Batch DOM reads, then writes. Animate with transform and opacity (compositor only).
  • Main thread: break long tasks (over 50 ms) into chunks, or move them to a Web Worker.
  • V8 also caches compiled code for scripts that load repeatedly.

Honest note: measure with the Performance panel before you optimize. In most web apps, network, bundle size and DOM work cost far more than micro-optimizations of JavaScript.

Follow-up: "What is a long task?" Answer: any main-thread task longer than 50 ms. During a long task, the page cannot respond to input. It hurts the INP (Interaction to Next Paint) metric.

Q30

When to use Web Workers

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

A Web Worker runs a script on a background thread with its own event loop and global scope (self). It has no access to the DOM, window or document. It communicates with the main thread through messages.

Data transfer options:

Method Cost Note
postMessage(data) Structured clone: copy Slow for large data. Functions cannot be sent.
postMessage(buf, [buf]) Transfer: no copy The sender loses access to the ArrayBuffer
SharedArrayBuffer + Atomics Shared memory Needs cross-origin isolation headers (COOP/COEP)

Use a worker when a task blocks the main thread for more than about 50 ms:

  • Parse or transform large JSON, CSV or Excel files.
  • Image and video processing, canvas filters (with OffscreenCanvas).
  • Compression, encryption, hashing large files before upload.
  • Search indexing, sorting and filtering very large lists on the client.
  • ML inference (TensorFlow.js, ONNX Runtime Web), syntax highlighting, Markdown parsing.

Do not use a worker for:

  • Network requests: fetch is already async.
  • Small tasks: starting a worker and cloning messages costs more than the work.
  • DOM updates: the worker cannot touch the DOM.

Other worker types:

  • Shared Worker: one worker shared by several tabs of the same origin.
  • Service Worker: a network proxy for offline support, caching and push notifications. It is not for CPU work.
  • Node.js: worker_threads for CPU work (the event loop is single-threaded too).

Tooling: libraries like Comlink make a worker look like an async object, so you call await api.parse(text) instead of handling raw messages.

Follow-up: "Does async/await make CPU work non-blocking?" Answer: no. async only helps code that waits for I/O. A CPU loop inside an async function still blocks the thread. CPU work needs a worker or must be split into chunks.

Advanced Concepts

6 questions
Q31

Immutability and why it matters

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Immutability means a value does not change after you create it. To "change" it, you create a new value that contains the change. Primitives (string, number, boolean) are always immutable. Objects and arrays are mutable by default, so immutability for them is a discipline.

Immutable array operations: map, filter, concat, slice, spread, and the ES2023 methods toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced, with(index, value). Mutating ones to avoid on shared data: push, pop, splice, sort, reverse, fill.

Why it matters:

  1. Predictable code: a function cannot change data that other code depends on. Shared-reference bugs disappear.
  2. Cheap change detection: compare references, not deep contents. prev !== next means something changed. React (useState, memo, dependency arrays) and Redux depend on this. If you mutate state, React may not re-render.
  3. History: undo/redo and time-travel debugging keep old versions for free.
  4. Safer concurrency and caching: immutable data can be shared and memoized without defensive copies.

Costs and tools:

  • More allocation and copying. For deep updates, the spread syntax becomes noisy.
  • Immer lets you write mutating code on a draft and produces an immutable result: produce(state, (d) => { d.user.name = 'B'; }). Redux Toolkit uses it.
  • Object.freeze enforces immutability at runtime (shallow). TypeScript readonly enforces it at compile time.

Trap: const does not make a value immutable. const arr = []; arr.push(1) works. const only blocks reassignment of the variable.

Follow-up: "Why does React require immutable state updates?" Answer: React compares the old and new state by reference (Object.is). A mutated object has the same reference, so React thinks nothing changed and skips the render.

Q32

Pure functions

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

A function is pure if both conditions are true:

  1. Deterministic: the same arguments always give the same result.
  2. No side effects: it does not change anything outside itself and does not depend on outside state that can change.

Side effects include: changing arguments, global or module variables, the DOM, network requests, file or database I/O, logging, reading Date.now(), Math.random() or mutable outer variables, and throwing based on external state.

Benefits:

  • Testing: no mocks or setup. Input → expected output.
  • Memoization: results can be cached by arguments (useMemo, reselect, React.memo rely on purity).
  • Referential transparency: you can replace a call with its result. This makes reasoning and refactoring safe.
  • Parallel or reordered execution is safe.

Real programs need side effects. The design goal is "functional core, imperative shell": keep business logic pure (calculate price, validate input, transform data) and keep side effects at the edges (route handlers, services, effects).

React rule: component render functions and reducers must be pure. Side effects go in event handlers or useEffect. Strict Mode calls render twice in development to expose impure renders.

Follow-up: "Is a function that uses a local mutable variable pure?" Answer: yes, if the mutation is local and invisible from outside. Purity is about observable behavior.

Q33

Monolithic vs modular JS architecture

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Monolithic JavaScript: the application lives in a few large files, or many files that share global variables (old <script> tags in a fixed order). Everything can touch everything.

Modular JavaScript: code is split into modules. Each module has its own scope, exports a small public API and imports what it needs explicitly.

Monolithic Modular
Scope Shared global scope, name collisions Each module has a private scope
Dependencies Implicit (script order) Explicit import graph
Coupling High: a change can break distant code Low, if module boundaries are good
Testing Hard to isolate a part Import and test one module
Loading One large bundle Tree shaking removes unused exports; import() loads features on demand
Team scale Merge conflicts, unclear ownership Teams own modules or packages
Reuse Copy-paste Import or publish as a package

Module systems history: globals and IIFEs → CommonJS (Node) and AMD → ES Modules (the standard, Q64).

Good modular structure:

  • Organize by feature or domain (users/, orders/), not by technical type (controllers/, utils/ for everything).
  • Each feature exposes an index.js public API. Other features import only from it.
  • Avoid circular imports. They cause undefined values during initialization.
  • Keep shared code small and stable.

The same trade-off exists at larger scale: a monolithic frontend vs micro-frontends, and a monolithic backend vs microservices. Honest view: a well-structured modular monolith is the right default for most teams. Splitting into separately deployed parts adds network calls, versioning and operations work. Do it only when team or scaling problems demand it.

Follow-up: "What is tree shaking and what breaks it?" Answer: the bundler removes exports that nothing imports, using the static ESM import graph. CommonJS, side effects at module top level, and re-exporting everything through barrel files can prevent it. Mark packages "sideEffects": false when safe.

Q34

Event delegation and its benefits

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

DOM events bubble: an event on a child element travels up through each ancestor to document and window. Event delegation uses this. You attach one listener to a common ancestor and decide in the handler which child started the event.

Why closest: e.target can be an icon or a <span> inside the button. closest walks up to the element you care about.

Event phases: capture (window → target), target, bubble (target → window). addEventListener(type, fn, true) or { capture: true } listens in the capture phase.

Benefits:

  • Memory and setup: 1 listener instead of 1,000 for a long list.
  • Dynamic content: elements added later work automatically. No re-binding after each render.
  • Less cleanup: removing a row does not leave a listener behind.
  • Central logic for related actions.

Limits:

  • Some events do not bubble: focus, blur, mouseenter, mouseleave, load. Use focusin/focusout, mouseover/mouseout, or capture.
  • A child handler that calls e.stopPropagation() breaks delegation for that event.
  • Very frequent events (mousemove, scroll) on a high ancestor run the handler often. Keep it cheap.

Real use: React attaches its event listeners at the root container and dispatches internally. jQuery's $(parent).on('click', '.child', fn) is delegation.

Follow-up: "What is the difference between stopPropagation and preventDefault?" Answer: stopPropagation stops the event from moving to other elements. preventDefault stops the browser's default action (link navigation, form submit). They are independent.

Q35

Symbols and real-world use cases

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Symbol is a primitive type (ES2015). Each symbol is unique and immutable. The description is only a label for debugging.

Symbols as property keys:

Symbol keys are hidden from normal iteration but not private. For real privacy, use #private class fields or closures.

Real-world use cases:

  1. Collision-free metadata on objects you do not own. A library can tag objects without any risk of clashing with user keys.
  2. Unique constants:
  1. Well-known symbols change built-in behavior:

Others: Symbol.asyncIterator (for await), Symbol.toStringTag (custom Object.prototype.toString output), Symbol.hasInstance (custom instanceof).

  1. Frameworks: React marks its elements with $$typeof: Symbol.for('react.element'). JSON cannot contain a symbol, so a JSON payload from a server cannot inject a fake React element (an XSS protection).

Follow-up: "Can you convert a symbol to a string implicitly?" Answer: no. '' + sym throws TypeError. Use String(sym) or sym.description.

Q36

How Proxy works and when you would use it

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

A Proxy wraps a target object and lets you intercept fundamental operations on it. You define traps in a handler object. Operations without a trap go to the target unchanged.

Main traps:

Trap Intercepts
get(target, key, receiver) proxy.x, proxy[key]
set(target, key, value, receiver) proxy.x = v (must return true, or it throws in strict mode)
has(target, key) key in proxy
deleteProperty(target, key) delete proxy.x
ownKeys(target) Object.keys, for...in, Reflect.ownKeys
apply(target, thisArg, args) Calls, when the target is a function
construct(target, args) new proxy()

Reflect has one method for each trap with the same arguments. Use it to perform the default behavior inside a trap. It also handles getters and inheritance correctly through receiver.

Use cases with code:

Other uses: logging and profiling access, read-only views, access control, test mocks and spies, API clients where any method name becomes a request (api.users.get()), and Immer drafts.

Limits:

  • Slower than direct property access. Avoid in hot loops.
  • proxy !== target. Code that compares identity or uses the target as a WeakMap key may break.
  • Built-ins with internal slots (Map, Set, Date) and private class fields (#x) fail through a proxy, because their methods check the real object. Wrap methods with .bind(target) to fix it.
  • Proxies are shallow. Nested objects need their own proxies (Vue creates them lazily in get).
  • Invariants: a trap cannot lie about non-configurable properties. The engine throws if it does.

Follow-up: "Proxy vs Object.defineProperty getters/setters?" Answer: defineProperty works per property and cannot detect new or deleted properties or array index changes. A Proxy intercepts all of them. This is why Vue 3 switched from defineProperty (Vue 2) to Proxy.

TypeScript: Types & Interfaces

7 questions
Q37

Difference between type and interface

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Both can describe the shape of an object, and for most object types they are interchangeable.

What only type can do:

What only interface can do — declaration merging:

This is how you augment library types (Express Request, Window, ProcessEnv). A type with the same name twice is an error.

Extension differences:

extends checks compatibility early and gives clearer errors. & silently produces never properties.

interface type
Object shapes Yes Yes
Unions, tuples, primitives, mapped, conditional No Yes
Declaration merging Yes No
Extend extends (checked) & (can create never)
Class implements Yes Yes, if it resolves to an object type
Error messages Shows the interface name Can show the expanded structure

Practical rule: use interface for public object contracts and anything that may need augmentation. Use type for unions, tuples, function types and computed types. The TypeScript team's own advice is close to this. In an interview, say that consistency within a codebase matters more than the choice.

Follow-up: "Can an interface extend a type?" Answer: yes, if the type is an object type (or an intersection of object types). It cannot extend a union.

Q38

When to use union vs intersection types

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Union A | B = "one of these." Intersection A & B = "all of these at the same time."

Union:

With a union, you can use only members common to all options until you narrow (with typeof, in, instanceof, equality, or a discriminant, Q59).

Use unions for: alternatives and variants ('GET' | 'POST'), optional values (User | null), API results (Success | Failure), function parameters that accept several input forms.

Intersection:

Use intersections for: combining small reusable shapes, mixins, adding fields to an existing type (props + extra props in React wrappers).

Set theory view (helps in interviews): a type is a set of values. A union is the set union, so it accepts more values and you know less about each. An intersection is the set intersection, so it accepts fewer values and each value has more members.

Traps:

  • string & number is never: no value is both.
  • Intersecting object types with the same key and different types gives that key type never, and the object becomes impossible to create.
  • keyof (A | B) = only the common keys. keyof (A & B) = all keys. People often expect the opposite.

Follow-up: "What does string | never simplify to?" Answer: string. never is the empty set, so it disappears from unions.

Q39

Type inference in TypeScript

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Type inference is the compiler's ability to work out types from the code without explicit annotations.

Where inference happens:

Widening and narrowing:

  • let s = 'a' widens to string, because a let can change.
  • const s = 'a' stays 'a'.
  • Object properties widen: const o = { method: 'GET' } gives method: string. This breaks code that expects 'GET' | 'POST'.
  • Fix with as const (deep readonly literals) or satisfies:

Control-flow narrowing is also inference: after if (x !== null), the compiler knows x is not null inside the block.

When to annotate:

  • Function parameters: always. They cannot be inferred (except in callbacks with context).
  • Exported functions and public API return types: yes. This prevents accidental return type changes and speeds up the compiler.
  • Empty initial values: const list: User[] = [] (otherwise never[] or any[]). useState<User | null>(null) in React.
  • Local variables with clear initializers: no. Let inference work.

Follow-up: "What is the difference between as const and satisfies?" Answer: as const makes literals readonly and narrow. satisfies checks a value against a type without changing the inferred type. You can combine them: {...} as const satisfies Config.

Q40

Optional chaining and nullish coalescing

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Both are JavaScript operators (ES2020). TypeScript understands them for narrowing and can compile them to older JavaScript.

Optional chaining ?.: stop and return undefined if the value on the left is null or undefined.

Short-circuit: if user is null, nothing to the right runs. a?.b.c() does not evaluate .c(). Side effects in the rest of the chain do not happen.

Nullish coalescing ??: use the right side only when the left side is null or undefined.

?? vs ||:

Left value x || 'default' x ?? 'default'
undefined / null 'default' 'default'
0 'default' (often a bug) 0
'' 'default' ''
false 'default' false
NaN 'default' NaN

Assignment form: options.timeout ??= 5000 assigns only if the value is nullish. Also ||= and &&=.

Rules and traps:

  • You cannot mix ?? with || or && without parentheses: a || b ?? c is a syntax error. Write (a || b) ?? c.
  • Overuse of ?. hides bugs. If user must exist at this point, user?.name silently gives undefined instead of failing early. Use ?. only where absence is valid.
  • The result type includes undefined: user?.name has type string | undefined.
  • ?. cannot be used on the left side of an assignment: user?.name = 'x' is an error.

Follow-up: "How do you give a default for a nested optional value?" Answer: combine them: const theme = settings?.ui?.theme ?? 'light'.

Q41

Difference between any, unknown and never

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

any: switches type checking off for this value. Anything can be assigned to it, and it can be assigned to anything and used in any way.

unknown: the safe top type. Anything can be assigned to it, but you must narrow it before you use it.

never: the bottom type. The set of no values. Nothing (except never) can be assigned to it, and it can be assigned to everything.

any unknown never
Position Escape hatch (top and bottom at once) Top type Bottom type
Assign any value to it Yes Yes No
Assign it to other types Yes Only to unknown / any Yes
Use members without checks Yes No Not applicable
Typical use Migration, quick hacks Untrusted input, catch, generic containers Exhaustive checks, functions that throw, type filtering

Rule: never use any for external data. Use unknown and validate it (Q57, Q58). any is contagious: one any can spread through inferred types into large parts of the codebase without any error.

Follow-up: "Where does never appear without you writing it?" Answer: after narrowing removes all options, for an empty array inside an object literal (never[]), and for impossible intersections like string & number.

Q42

How structural typing works

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

TypeScript uses structural typing: two types are compatible if their shapes are compatible. Names and declarations do not matter. Java and C# use nominal typing, where the declared name decides.

Rule: a value of type S can be assigned to type T if S has at least all the required members of T, with compatible types.

Excess property check — the exception for fresh object literals:

TypeScript assumes an extra property in a literal written in place is probably a typo. Assign the literal to a variable first and the check does not apply.

Functions are structural too:

This is why arr.forEach((item) => ...) works even though forEach passes three arguments.

Problem: different meanings with the same shape are mixed silently.

Solution: branded (nominal-like) types:

Classes with private or #private members are compared nominally for those members: two classes with the same private field are not compatible.

Follow-up: "Why did TypeScript choose structural typing?" Answer: JavaScript code uses object literals and duck typing everywhere. Structural typing describes how JavaScript is actually written.

Q43

What readonly is and how it is enforced

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Forms of readonly in TypeScript:

How it is enforced: only by the compiler. The emitted JavaScript has no readonly protection. At runtime, anything can change the object.

Limits to know:

  1. Shallow: Readonly<User> does not protect nested objects. user.address.city = 'x' compiles.
  1. Aliasing hole: a readonly type can be assigned to a mutable type with the same shape, and then changed:

(Readonly arrays are stricter: readonly string[] cannot be assigned to string[].)

  1. Type assertions and any can bypass it.

readonly vs const: const is about a variable binding. readonly is about a property or array type.

readonly vs Object.freeze: freeze works at runtime but is shallow and has no compile-time benefit by itself. TypeScript types the result of Object.freeze(obj) as Readonly<typeof obj>, so using both gives compile-time and runtime protection.

Follow-up: "Why mark function parameters readonly?" Answer: it documents and enforces that the function does not mutate its input, and it lets callers pass readonly arrays (a readonly array cannot be passed to a parameter typed string[]).
