Generic constraints

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

A generic type parameter T accepts any type by default. Inside the function, you can then do almost nothing with a T value, because TypeScript cannot assume any members. A constraint (T extends X) limits T to types assignable to X, so you can use the members of X.

Why not just (x: { length: number })? Because a generic keeps the exact type for the return value:

keyof constraint — the most common pattern:

Other constraint examples:

Trap: a constraint is a lower bound of capability, not the exact type. You cannot return a new object literal as T:

Follow-up: "What is the difference between T extends string and a string parameter?" Answer: T extends string keeps the literal type: calling with 'admin' gives T = 'admin', so the return type can be 'admin'. A plain string parameter loses it.

Q45

How TypeScript infers generics in functions

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

When you call a generic function without explicit type arguments, TypeScript infers them from the arguments.

Process (simplified):

  1. For each parameter that uses a type parameter, compare the argument's type with the parameter's type and collect candidates for T.
  2. Combine the candidates. With several candidates, pick a best common type, or report an error if they conflict.
  3. If no candidate is found, use the default (Q48), else the constraint, else unknown.
  4. Check the arguments against the result.

Contextual flow, left to right:

If a callback comes before the data argument, inference can fail. API designers put the data first for this reason.

Keeping literal types — const type parameters (TS 5.0+):

Blocking an inference site — NoInfer<T> (TS 5.4+):

When inference fails or is too wide, pass the type explicitly: useState<User | null>(null), new Map<string, number>().

Follow-up: "Why does useState(null) cause problems in React + TS?" Answer: T is inferred as null, so you can never set a User. Write useState<User | null>(null).

Q46

Function overloads

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Overloads let one function have several call signatures, so the return type can depend on the argument types in ways a single signature cannot express.

Structure: overload signatures (visible to callers) + one implementation signature (hidden) with the body.

With a single signature (input: string | string[]): HTMLElement | null | (HTMLElement | null)[], every caller would get the wide union and need casts.

Rules:

  1. Callers see only the overload signatures. The implementation signature must be compatible with all of them, but it is not callable directly.
  2. TypeScript picks the first overload that matches, from top to bottom. Put the most specific overloads first.
  3. The compiler does not verify that the body returns the right type for each overload. The implementation is checked only against its own wide signature. Overloads can lie.
  4. Overloads exist only in types. The emitted JavaScript has one function.

Overloads in other places:

Alternatives that are often better:

The TypeScript handbook advice: prefer union parameters over overloads when possible.

Follow-up: "Where do you see overloads in the standard library?" Answer: document.createElement ('div' → HTMLDivElement, 'input' → HTMLInputElement), addEventListener, and Array.prototype.reduce.

Q47

Difference between void and never return types

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

void: the function returns normally, but its return value has no meaning (it is undefined).

never: the function never returns normally. It always throws, loops forever, or ends the process.

Why never is useful — control-flow analysis:

The void substitutability rule (a common follow-up):

A function type that returns void accepts functions that return anything, because the caller promises to ignore the value. But a function declaration with an explicit : void return type cannot return a value:

Other differences:

void never
Meaning Returns, value is irrelevant Does not return
Values undefined None
Assignable to other types No (only to void, unknown, any) Yes, to every type
Inferred for Functions with no return Function expressions that only throw. (Function declarations that only throw are inferred as void — annotate never explicitly.)

undefined vs void return: use undefined when callers may check the value. Use void for "do not use the result."

Follow-up: "What is the return type of an async function that only throws?" Answer: Promise<never>.

Q48

Default generic type

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

A default type argument is used when the caller does not provide the type argument and TypeScript cannot infer it.

Rules:

  1. Parameters with defaults must come after required parameters: <T, U = string> is valid, <T = string, U> is not.
  2. A default must satisfy its constraint: <T extends object = {}>.
  3. A default can reference earlier parameters: <T, K extends keyof T = keyof T>.
  4. Inference wins over the default. The default applies only when there is nothing to infer from.

Real examples:

Choose a safe default. unknown forces callers to validate. any as a default silently disables checks for everyone who forgets the type argument.

Follow-up: "When is a default generic better than overloads?" Answer: when one signature covers both the simple and the advanced case, and the only difference is how precise the type is.

TypeScript: Advanced Types

7 questions
Q49

Mapped types with an example

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

A mapped type creates a new object type by iterating over a union of keys and computing a property type for each key. Syntax: { [K in Keys]: Type }.

The usual form maps over the keys of an existing type with keyof, and reads each property type with T[K] (indexed access):

Modifiers: + adds, - removes. readonly and ? can be changed:

Key remapping with as (TS 4.1+): rename, filter or compute keys.

Practical example — form errors typed from the form shape:

Homomorphic mapped types (those over keyof T) keep the original readonly and ? modifiers, and they distribute over unions and preserve arrays and tuples.

Follow-up: "Why string & K in the template?" Answer: keyof T can include number and symbol keys. Template literal types accept only string-like types, so the intersection keeps only the string keys.

Q50

Conditional types

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

A conditional type chooses one of two types based on an assignability test:

If T is assignable to U, the result is X, else Y. It is a type-level if.

Distributive behavior: when the checked type is a naked type parameter and you pass a union, the condition runs once for each member, and the results are joined in a union.

never disappears from unions, so returning never for a member removes it. This is how filtering works.

To stop distribution, wrap both sides in a tuple:

Special case: never passed to a distributive conditional gives never (an empty union has no members to map). Wrap in [T] to test for never: type IsNever<T> = [T] extends [never] ? true : false.

Conditional types become powerful with infer (Q51) and recursion:

Practical uses: return types that depend on inputs, library typings (React prop extraction, ORM query results), filtering unions, safe API result types.

Warning: deeply nested conditional types are hard to read and slow to compile. If a teammate cannot understand it in a minute, simplify it.

Follow-up: "When is a conditional type deferred?" Answer: when it depends on a generic parameter that is not yet known (inside a generic function). TypeScript cannot pick a branch, so it keeps the conditional type unresolved until the type is concrete.

Q51

How infer works

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

infer declares a new type variable inside the extends clause of a conditional type. If the match succeeds, TypeScript sets that variable to the part of the type at that position. You can use it only in the true branch.

More positions where infer works:

Constraint on infer (TS 4.7+):

Real-world use: get the type of what a function returns without exporting a separate type.

The built-ins ReturnType, Parameters, InstanceType, ConstructorParameters and Awaited are all implemented with infer.

Follow-up: "What happens if the same infer variable appears in two places?" Answer: TypeScript collects candidates from both positions. In covariant positions (like return types), it creates a union. In contravariant positions (function parameters), it creates an intersection.

Q52

Partial, Required, Pick, Omit, Record

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

These are built-in utility types, implemented as mapped types.

Utility Definition Result with User
Partial<T> { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] } All four properties optional
Required<T> { [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] } email becomes required
Pick<T, K extends keyof T> { [P in K]: T[P] } Pick<User, 'id' | 'name'> → { id; name }
Omit<T, K extends keyof any> Pick<T, Exclude<keyof T, K>> Omit<User, 'passwordHash'> → { id; name; email? }
Record<K extends keyof any, V> { [P in K]: V } Record<'admin' | 'user', string[]>

Real uses:

Traps:

  1. Omit does not require K to be a real key (K extends keyof any). Omit<User, 'pasword'> compiles and removes nothing. Some teams define a strict version: type StrictOmit<T, K extends keyof T> = Omit<T, K>.
  2. Omit on a union type is not distributive. Omit<A | B, 'x'> keeps only the common keys. Use a distributive helper: type DistOmit<T, K extends PropertyKey> = T extends any ? Omit<T, K> : never.
  3. All of them are shallow.
  4. Record<string, V> claims every string key exists. Reading a missing key gives V, not V | undefined, unless noUncheckedIndexedAccess is on.
  5. Partial accepts {}. It does not guarantee that at least one field is present.

Other built-ins worth knowing: Readonly, Exclude, Extract, NonNullable, ReturnType, Parameters, Awaited, InstanceType, and the string ones (Uppercase, Capitalize).

Follow-up: "Implement Pick." Answer: type MyPick<T, K extends keyof T> = { [P in K]: T[P] }.

Q53

Template literal types

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Template literal types use the JavaScript template string syntax at the type level to build string literal types.

Intrinsic string helpers: Uppercase<S>, Lowercase<S>, Capitalize<S>, Uncapitalize<S>.

Pattern placeholders: ${number}, ${string}, ${bigint}, ${boolean}.

Parsing strings with infer:

This is how typed routers (Express typings, TanStack Router) check route parameters.

With mapped types (Q49) they generate API shapes: getters, event handler names, typed object paths ('address.city' for forms, Q66).

Limits:

  • Cross products grow fast: three unions of 10 members make 1,000 members. TypeScript stops at 100,000 and slows long before that.
  • Recursive parsing types are hard to debug and have recursion depth limits.
  • They check string shapes only. '99999px' is a valid ${number}px.

Follow-up: "Can template literal types validate an email?" Answer: only crudely (${string}@${string}.${string}). Real validation needs runtime checks.

Q54

keyof and typeof together

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

typeof in a type position gets the TypeScript type of a value (a variable, constant, object or function). It is different from the JavaScript runtime typeof operator, which returns a string.

keyof takes a type and gives the union of its property names.

The main pattern: one runtime object is the single source of truth, and the types follow it. You write the data once.

Without as const, Role would be string, because object property values widen.

This pattern is a common replacement for enum: it emits a plain object, works with type stripping tools, and gives a literal union.

From arrays:

The array version also gives you a runtime list for validation and dropdowns.

From functions:

Trap: keyof on a type with an index signature gives string | number (number keys are allowed because JavaScript converts them to strings).

Follow-up: "Why can't you write keyof config directly?" Answer: config is a value. keyof needs a type, so you first convert the value with typeof.

Q55

Index signature and its limitations

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

An index signature describes an object whose keys are not known in advance but whose values share a type.

The key name (studentId) is only documentation.

Limitations:

  1. All named properties must match the index signature's value type.
  1. Reads are unsafe by default. Every key is assumed to exist:

Enable noUncheckedIndexedAccess in tsconfig.json. Then scores['missing'] is number | undefined, and you must check it. This flag also affects arrays (arr[0] becomes T | undefined).

  1. Allowed key types: string, number, symbol, template literal patterns ([key: `data-${string}`]: string) and unions of these. A union of literals ('a' | 'b') is not allowed. Use a mapped type or Record<'a' | 'b', V> instead, which also requires all keys to be present.
  2. number keys are a subset of string keys. JavaScript converts obj[1] to obj['1']. If you have both, the number index type must be assignable to the string index type.
  3. No autocomplete and no typo detection for keys. config.prot compiles if config has a string index signature.
  4. Excess property checks disappear, because any extra key matches the signature.

Better alternatives:

Need Use
Known, fixed set of keys Record<Union, V> or an interface
Truly dynamic keys, frequent add and delete Map<K, V> (has .has(), .size, safe iteration, any key type)
Mostly known keys plus some extras Named properties plus an index signature with a wider value type
Dynamic keys, safe reads Index signature + noUncheckedIndexedAccess

Follow-up: "What is the difference between Record<string, V> and { [k: string]: V }?" Answer: they are effectively the same type. Record is a mapped type that produces that index signature when K is string.

TypeScript: Type Safety & Architecture

5 questions
Q56

How TypeScript helps prevent runtime errors

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

TypeScript analyzes the code before it runs and rejects programs that would use values in invalid ways. Errors move from production (runtime) to the editor (compile time).

Error classes it catches:

It also prevents misuse of APIs through precise types: literal unions instead of free strings, readonly data, discriminated unions that make invalid states unrepresentable (Q59).

What TypeScript does not catch:

  1. External data. Types are erased at runtime (Q62). An API response, JSON.parse, localStorage, process.env, form input or a database row can have any shape. const user: User = await res.json() is a claim, not a check.
  2. Escape hatches: any, as assertions, ! non-null assertions, @ts-ignore. Each one switches the checker off at that point.
  3. Unsound areas by design: array and index access without noUncheckedIndexedAccess (arr[10] is typed T), method parameter bivariance, mutable array covariance (Dog[] assigned to Animal[], then a Cat pushed in).
  4. Logic errors: wrong calculations, wrong business rules, race conditions, infinite loops, performance problems.
  5. Errors inside untyped or wrongly typed third-party code.

How to get the full benefit:

  • "strict": true and noUncheckedIndexedAccess.
  • Runtime validation at every boundary (Q57, Q58).
  • Lint rules against any and floating promises.
  • Tests for logic. Types and tests cover different classes of bugs.

Evidence often quoted: a 2017 study of public JavaScript bugs ("To Type or Not to Type") found that TypeScript or Flow annotations would have detected about 15% of them. The real value grows with codebase size, refactoring frequency and team size.

Follow-up: "So is TypeScript worth it if it catches only part of the bugs?" Answer: yes for most teams. The cost is low per bug caught, and the editor support, safe refactoring and documentation value come in addition.

Q57

How to type API responses safely

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

The unsafe version is everywhere:

If the backend renames a field, returns null, or sends an error object with status 200, the code fails later, far from the cause.

Correct approach: treat the body as unknown, validate at the boundary, and derive the static type from the runtime schema so the two cannot drift.

Alternatives and complements:

Approach How Trade-off
Schema validation (Zod, Valibot, ArkType, Yup) Runtime check + inferred type Small runtime cost, bundle size
Code generation from OpenAPI (openapi-typescript, orval) Types and client generated from the backend contract Types only — still add validation for trust
GraphQL codegen Types generated from schema and queries Requires GraphQL
End-to-end typing (tRPC) Client infers types from server code TypeScript on both sides, same repo
Typed error results Return Result<T, E> instead of throwing More explicit handling at call sites

Model errors explicitly too:

Performance note: validate once at the boundary, not on every access. For very large payloads on hot paths, validate a sample in production and everything in development, and document that decision.

Follow-up: "Why not just trust the backend if your team owns it?" Answer: deployments are not atomic. An old frontend can talk to a new backend, caches can serve old shapes, and bugs happen. Validation turns a silent corruption into a clear error at the boundary.

Q58

How to handle unknown backend data

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Rule: data from outside the program is unknown until proven otherwise. Prove it once at the boundary, convert it to a trusted domain type, and let the rest of the code trust that type. This principle is called "parse, don't validate."

Narrowing tools from simple to strong:

Trap: a hand-written type guard can lie. If isUser forgets to check name, TypeScript still trusts x is User. Schema libraries remove this risk because the type comes from the check itself.

Decide what happens on failure:

Situation Strategy
Required data is invalid Throw, show an error state, report to monitoring (Sentry) with the validation issues
Optional field is invalid Use a default and log a warning (.catch(default) in Zod)
List with some bad items Keep the valid items, drop and log the invalid ones
Unknown enum value from a newer backend Map to an 'unknown' variant instead of crashing

Also apply this to other untrusted inputs: process.env (validate once at startup and fail fast), localStorage (data from an old app version), URL query parameters, WebSocket messages, postMessage events, and request bodies on the server.

Follow-up: "What type does a catch variable have?" Answer: unknown with strict (useUnknownInCatchVariables), because anything can be thrown, not only Error. Narrow it with instanceof Error.

Q59

Discriminated unions and where they are useful

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

A discriminated (tagged) union is a union of object types where every member has a common property with a different literal type: the discriminant. Checking the discriminant narrows the value to one member.

Why this beats optional fields:

The union makes invalid states unrepresentable. You cannot create a success state without data or an error state without a message.

Exhaustiveness: if someone adds { status: 'cancelled' }, every switch with assertNever fails to compile until it handles the new case. The compiler finds all the places to update.

Where to use them:

  • UI request states and component variants ({ variant: 'link'; href } | { variant: 'button'; onClick }).
  • Redux/useReducer actions: { type: 'add'; item } | { type: 'remove'; id }.
  • Domain events and WebSocket messages: { kind: 'chat'; text } | { kind: 'typing'; userId }.
  • Result types instead of exceptions: { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E }.
  • Payment methods, shapes, AST nodes, notification types.

Rules:

  • The discriminant must be a literal type (string, number, boolean literal) present in every member.
  • Narrowing breaks if you destructure the discriminant away from the object in older TS versions. Since TS 4.6, destructured discriminants narrow too: const { status, ...rest } = state then if (status === 'success').
  • Validate external data with a schema that matches the union (z.discriminatedUnion('status', [...])).

Follow-up: "How does this relate to pattern matching in other languages?" Answer: it is the TypeScript version of algebraic data types (sum types) in Rust, Haskell or Swift enums with associated values. The switch plus never check gives exhaustive matching.

Q60

How to enforce strict typing in large codebases

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Strictness has to be enforced by tools and process, not by good intentions.

  1. Compiler settings (tsconfig.json):

strict turns on noImplicitAny, strictNullChecks, strictFunctionTypes, strictBindCallApply, strictPropertyInitialization, noImplicitThis, alwaysStrict and useUnknownInCatchVariables. Share one base config across packages (extends).

  1. Linting with typescript-eslint (strict-type-checked preset):
  • no-explicit-any, no-unsafe-assignment, no-unsafe-member-access, no-unsafe-call, no-unsafe-return — stop any from spreading.
  • no-floating-promises, no-misused-promises — async bugs.
  • ban-ts-comment — forbid @ts-ignore, allow @ts-expect-error only with a description (it fails when the error disappears, so it cannot rot).
  • no-non-null-assertion, consistent-type-assertions — limit ! and as.
  • switch-exhaustiveness-check.
  1. CI gates: tsc --noEmit (or tsc -b with project references) and ESLint must pass before merge. A local editor is not enforcement. Use pre-commit hooks for speed, CI for truth.
  2. Boundaries: runtime validation for HTTP requests and responses, environment variables, queues and storage (Q57, Q58). Shared schemas between services (Q67).
  3. Architecture: branded types for IDs and money, discriminated unions for states, no exported any, explicit return types on public module APIs.
  4. Review culture: every as, ! and eslint-disable needs a reason in the code or the PR. Track counts.
  5. Legacy code: turn strictness on gradually.
  • Project references or separate tsconfig files per package, with strict on for new packages first.
  • Tools like betterer record the current error count and fail CI only if it increases (ratchet).
  • Fix one flag at a time across the codebase (strictNullChecks is usually the largest).
  1. Performance at scale: project references and incremental builds keep type checking fast, so people do not disable it. Very complex types slow the editor for everyone.

Follow-up: "How do you handle a legitimate need for any?" Answer: isolate it in one small, well-tested function with a typed signature (for example, a wrapper around an untyped library), add a comment and a disable for that line, and keep any out of the exported types.

TypeScript + JavaScript Internals

5 questions
Q61

How TypeScript compiles to JavaScript

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

The official compiler tsc runs this pipeline:

  1. Scanner (lexer): source text → tokens (const, identifier, =, number...).
  2. Parser: tokens → an abstract syntax tree (AST). Syntax errors appear here.
  3. Binder: walks the AST, creates symbols for every declaration, connects uses to declarations, builds scopes and the control-flow graph used for narrowing.
  4. Checker: resolves types, infers, checks assignability, narrows. This is the largest and slowest part, and it produces the type errors.
  5. Transformer and emitter: removes type syntax, converts newer syntax to the target version (for example, optional chaining for ES2019), converts modules to the module format, and writes .js, .d.ts (with declaration) and .map files.

Important facts:

  • Type checking and emit are independent. tsc writes JavaScript even when there are type errors, unless noEmitOnError is set. A type error does not change the output.
  • target controls syntax conversion only. It does not add polyfills for missing runtime APIs (Array.prototype.at, Promise.any). That is the job of lib (which declares what types exist) plus a polyfill if you need one.
  • Fast tools strip types without checking: esbuild, swc, Babel, Vite, Bun, and Node.js type stripping (Node 22.6+ behind a flag; on by default in newer versions). They transform each file alone, so set isolatedModules: true. Run tsc --noEmit separately in CI and in the editor for checking.
  • Erasable vs non-erasable syntax: most TypeScript syntax can be deleted to get valid JavaScript. These features generate real code and cannot be simply stripped: enum, namespace with values, constructor parameter properties (constructor(private x: number)), legacy experimentalDecorators with metadata. erasableSyntaxOnly (TS 5.8+) forbids them, so the code runs with plain type stripping.
  • Microsoft is porting the compiler to native code in Go ("TypeScript 7") for large speedups in type checking and editor responsiveness. The language rules stay the same.

Follow-up: "Why is tsc slow on large projects and how do you speed it up?" Answer: the checker must resolve the full type graph. Use incremental and project references (tsc -b), skipLibCheck, explicit return types on exported functions, simpler types, and a fast transpiler for dev builds with tsc --noEmit in parallel.

Q62

What happens to types at runtime

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Nothing. TypeScript erases all type information when it emits JavaScript. Types exist only for the compiler and the editor. This is called type erasure.

Consequences:

  1. No runtime type checks. as User does not validate anything. Wrong data flows through until something crashes.
  2. You cannot test against a type:
  1. Generics have no runtime value. You cannot write new T(), T.name or if (value is T). Pass a constructor, a factory or a schema as a real argument:
  1. Overloads collapse into one function. Private TypeScript members (private x) are normal public JavaScript properties at runtime. Only #x is truly private.

What does exist at runtime:

  • class declarations: real constructor functions, so instanceof MyClass works.
  • enum: a real object (except const enum, which is inlined).
  • Decorators: real function calls. With emitDecoratorMetadata and reflect-metadata, the compiler emits parameter type metadata for classes (design:paramtypes). NestJS and Angular use this for dependency injection. It works only for class types, not interfaces.

Bridging the gap — get runtime checks and static types from one source:

  • Schema-first libraries: Zod, Valibot, ArkType, io-ts (z.infer).
  • Code generation from OpenAPI, GraphQL or JSON Schema.
  • Hand-written type guards (Q58).

Why TypeScript chose erasure: zero runtime cost, output that looks like hand-written JavaScript, and full compatibility with existing JavaScript libraries.

Follow-up: "How does NestJS know which service to inject if types are erased?" Answer: decorator metadata. emitDecoratorMetadata emits the constructor parameter classes as runtime values. Interfaces cannot be injected this way, which is why Nest uses injection tokens for them.

Q63

How TypeScript handles DOM typing

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

The DOM types come from lib.dom.d.ts, a large declaration file generated from the web specifications. tsconfig.json controls it:

If lib is not set, the default depends on target and includes DOM. For a Node-only project, remove DOM so code cannot use window or document by accident. Node types come from @types/node.

Element type hierarchy (simplified): EventTarget → Node → Element → HTMLElement → HTMLInputElement, HTMLButtonElement, HTMLCanvasElement... (and SVGElement for SVG).

Querying elements:

The tag name mapping comes from HTMLElementTagNameMap. For #id and .class selectors, TypeScript cannot know the element type.

Safe narrowing vs assertions:

Events:

Why e.target is EventTarget | null: with bubbling, the target can be any descendant, a text node, window, or a non-DOM object. TypeScript cannot know.

Custom events and globals:

In React, the types are different: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>, React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>, and useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null).

Follow-up: "Why does getElementById return HTMLElement but querySelector('#id') return Element?" Answer: IDs in an HTML document usually belong to HTML elements, so the declaration chose HTMLElement. querySelector can match SVG and other elements, so it returns the more general Element.

Q64

Difference between ESM and CommonJS in TypeScript projects

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Two module systems exist in the JavaScript world:

CommonJS ESM
Loading Synchronous, at runtime Asynchronous, graph analyzed before execution
Imports Dynamic: require anywhere, computed paths Static top-level import; dynamic import() returns a promise
Exports A mutable module.exports object (copies of values) Live bindings (importers see updated values)
Top-level await No Yes
Tree shaking Poor Good
__dirname, require Available Not available — use import.meta.dirname (Node 20.11+) or import.meta.url
Browser support No (needs a bundler) Native
Node file detection .cjs, or .js without "type": "module" .mjs, or .js with "type": "module" in package.json

TypeScript configuration:

With nodenext, TypeScript decides per file whether it is ESM or CJS, using package.json "type" and the extensions .mts (→ .mjs) and .cts (→ .cjs). It then enforces Node's rules:

  • In ESM, relative imports need the file extension of the output: import { x } from './util.js' (yes, .js in a .ts file).
  • import pkg from 'cjs-package' works only in the ways Node allows.

Interop settings and rules:

  • esModuleInterop (with allowSyntheticDefaultImports): lets you write import express from 'express' for a CJS package that uses module.exports = fn. Without it, you need import * as express from 'express'.
  • ESM can import CJS. Node exposes module.exports as the default export.
  • CJS loading ESM: historically only via await import(). Node 20.19+ and 22.12+ allow require() of synchronous ES modules (no top-level await).
  • verbatimModuleSyntax: TypeScript emits imports exactly as written, so you must use import type { User } for type-only imports. This avoids side-effect surprises when imports are elided.

Library publishing: dual packages use the exports field:

Risk: the dual package hazard. If one dependency loads the ESM copy and another loads the CJS copy, you get two instances (two singletons, failing instanceof). Many new libraries now ship ESM only.

Follow-up: "ERR_REQUIRE_ESM — what happened?" Answer: CommonJS code called require() on an ESM-only package in an older Node version. Fix: switch the project to ESM, use dynamic import(), upgrade Node, or pin an older CJS version of the package.

Q65

How to type third-party libraries without types

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Order of options:

  1. Check whether the package ships its own types (a types field in its package.json or .d.ts files). Most modern packages do.
  2. Check DefinitelyTyped: npm install -D @types/package-name. Scoped packages use @types/scope__name.
  3. Write your own declarations.
  4. As a last resort, declare the module as any.

Writing a declaration file:

Make sure tsconfig.json includes the file (for example, "include": ["src"]). Type only what you use. A partial, correct declaration is better than a complete, guessed one. Verify behavior against the library's documentation and source.

Quick escape (temporary):

Module augmentation — add to existing types:

Wrapping strategy: put the untyped library behind a small typed wrapper module in your code. The rest of the app imports only the wrapper. If the library changes or gets replaced, only one file changes, and any cannot spread.

Good practice: contribute the declarations back to DefinitelyTyped or to the library. Remember that declaration files are not checked against the real JavaScript. A wrong declaration is a source of false confidence.

Follow-up: "What is the difference between declare module 'x' in a global file and in a module file?" Answer: in a script file (no top-level import or export), it declares a new ambient module. In a module file, declare module 'x' augments the existing module 'x' instead of replacing it.

High-Signal System / Real-World Questions

5 questions

For these five questions, the interviewer scores your trade-off reasoning. Use this structure: state the goal, give a design, name what you gave up, and tie it to a project you built. A textbook answer with no experience behind it gets a weak score.

Q66

How would you design a type-safe form system?

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Goals: one definition of each form, compile-time errors for wrong field names, runtime validation of user input, typed submit data, typed error messages, and reuse of the same rules on the server.

Design:

  1. Schema as the single source of truth. A Zod (or Valibot) schema defines fields, types and rules. Types are derived from it, never written by hand.
  2. Separate input and output types. The input is what the inputs hold (strings). The output is what the submit handler receives after coercion and transforms.
  3. Typed field paths. Field names, including nested ones (address.city) and array items (items.0.qty), are a union type built from the schema. Wrong names fail at compile time.
  4. Typed errors keyed by path.
  5. Field components generic over the value type, so a number field cannot bind to a string path.
  6. The server validates the same schema. Client validation is for user experience. Server validation is for security.

In practice, do not build this from scratch. React Hook Form + @hookform/resolvers/zod gives typed register, typed errors and typed handleSubmit. TanStack Form is another option. In Next.js, the same schema can validate a Server Action.

Design decisions to mention:

  • When to validate: on blur for fields, on submit for the whole form, on change only after the first error (less noise).
  • Server errors: map API validation errors back to field paths with the same Path<T> type.
  • Dynamic forms (fields from a config): the schema is built at runtime, so static path types are weaker. Accept that, or generate types from the config.
  • Accessibility: connect errors with aria-describedby and aria-invalid. Types do not do this for you.

Follow-up: "Why not write the TypeScript interface and the validation separately?" Answer: they drift. Someone adds a field to the interface and forgets the validation, or the reverse. Deriving the type from the schema makes drift impossible.

Q67

How do you handle shared types between frontend and backend?

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

The goal is one contract that both sides compile against, plus runtime validation on the server, because shared types alone do not protect the server from bad requests.

Options:

Option How it works Best when Weak point
Shared schema package (monorepo) packages/contracts exports Zod schemas and inferred types. Frontend and backend import it. Both sides TypeScript, one repo or workspace Both apps must be rebuilt together; package versioning if repos are separate
End-to-end inference (tRPC, ts-rest, Hono RPC, oRPC) The client imports the server router's type and infers inputs and outputs Full-stack TS, one team, internal API Tight coupling; non-TS clients need a separate API layer
Contract-first OpenAPI An OpenAPI spec (written or generated from server code) → generated types and clients (openapi-typescript, orval) Public API, mobile apps, several languages Generation step in the build; spec can drift if hand-written
GraphQL Schema + graphql-codegen GraphQL backend GraphQL complexity

Example of the shared-schema approach:

Traps:

  • Share DTOs, not database models. A Prisma User type can contain passwordHash, internal flags and relation fields. Exposing it couples the UI to the database schema and risks leaking data.
  • JSON has no Date, Map, BigInt or undefined. Type the wire format (createdAt: string) and convert at the boundary.
  • Shared types do not replace server validation. A client can send anything with curl.
  • Old clients stay in use (mobile apps, cached tabs). Version the API and make additive changes (Q69).
  • Keep the contracts package free of server-only or browser-only code (no Prisma, no React), or one side will bundle the other side's dependencies.

Your answer (Quad). Say it in about 60 seconds:

  1. Setup: "In Quad, one shared package holds the Zod schemas for each API request and response. The Express backend and the Next.js frontend both import it."
  2. Backend: "Each Express route validates the request body with the schema before the handler runs. Bad input gets a 400 response, not a crash."
  3. Frontend: "The forms and the API client use the types from z.infer. A field rename in the schema breaks the build on both sides, so I find the problem before deploy."
  4. Boundary: "The schemas describe DTOs, not Prisma models. Prisma types stay inside the backend."
  5. Trade-off: "Both apps must build against the same package version. For a public API with non-TS clients, I would switch to OpenAPI."

Prepare for these follow-ups:

  • "How do you handle dates?" The JSON trap above. Know what Quad actually does.
  • "Why not tRPC?" tRPC couples the client to the server router. Zod schemas also work with a plain REST API and can produce an OpenAPI spec later.
  • "Show me." Have the shared package open on GitHub. If point 2 or point 4 is not true in your code today, fix the code before the interview, or do not claim it.
Q68

How would you refactor a large JS project to TypeScript?

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Principle: migrate incrementally while the product keeps shipping. A big-bang rewrite freezes features for months and usually fails.

Phase 0 — Prepare:

  • Get buy-in with a reason: bug classes you keep hitting, onboarding pain, refactoring fear. Not "TypeScript is popular."
  • Make sure tests and CI exist. They are your safety net, because the migration must not change behavior.

Phase 1 — Make TypeScript coexist with JavaScript:

  • The build accepts .js and .ts files together (Vite, Next.js and modern bundlers do this already).
  • Install @types/* for dependencies.
  • Add tsc --noEmit to CI immediately, even if it checks little at first.
  • Rule: all new files are .ts/.tsx.

Phase 2 — Convert files in a smart order:

  1. Shared types first: write the domain types (User, Order) and API types. They pay off everywhere.
  2. Boundaries next: the API client, database access, environment config. Add runtime validation there (Q57).
  3. Leaf modules (utilities with no internal imports), then upward through the dependency graph. Tools like madge show the graph.
  4. Rename .js → .ts in a separate commit from type fixes, so Git keeps file history.

Optional middle step: JSDoc types with // @ts-check give type checking without renaming files.

Phase 3 — Turn on strictness gradually:

  • One flag at a time: noImplicitAny → strictNullChecks (usually the biggest) → the rest of strict → noUncheckedIndexedAccess.
  • Use a ratchet so the error count can only go down (betterer, or a script comparing counts in CI).
  • Use unknown plus a // TODO(ts) comment instead of any. Track the number of any and @ts-expect-error as a metric.

Rules that keep it safe:

  • Never mix behavior changes and type migration in one PR. Reviewers cannot see a logic change hidden in a 2,000-line type diff.
  • Do not "fix" types with as everywhere. Each assertion hides a possible bug.
  • When TypeScript finds a real bug, fix it in a separate, clearly described PR.

Tools: ts-migrate (Airbnb) for automated first-pass conversion with any placeholders, typescript-eslint for rules, knip for unused exports found along the way.

How to measure progress: percentage of files in TS, number of any, strict flags enabled, and production errors of the types TS prevents (null access, undefined property).

Follow-up: "How long does it take?" Answer: it depends on size and team capacity. Present it as a background track (for example, 10–20% of each sprint, plus the new-files-in-TS rule), with visible metrics, rather than a fixed project with an end date.

Q69

How do you ensure backward compatibility in TS APIs?

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Two meanings: the TypeScript types a library exposes, and an HTTP API that TypeScript clients consume. Cover both.

A. Library public types (.d.ts)

The compatibility rules follow variance: consumers pass inputs (contravariant) and receive outputs (covariant).

Change Compatible? Reason
Add an optional parameter or optional input property Yes Old calls still valid
Add a required parameter or required input property No Old calls fail to compile
Widen a parameter type (string → string | number) Yes Accepts everything it accepted before
Narrow a parameter type No Some old calls rejected
Narrow a return type (string | null → string) Yes Callers' checks still work
Widen a return type, or add a member to a returned union No Consumers' exhaustive switch statements break
Add a member to an input union Yes
Add a property to a returned object Usually yes Breaks consumers who implement your interface
Remove or rename an export, type or property No
Make an interface stricter that users implement No Their implementations fail

Techniques:

  • Semantic versioning: a breaking type change is a major version, even if the JavaScript did not change.
  • Deprecate before removal:

Editors show deprecated APIs with strikethrough.

  • Keep the old signature as an overload while adding the new one.
  • Options objects instead of positional parameters: adding an optional property is easy; adding a positional parameter is fragile.
  • Detect changes automatically: API Extractor writes an API report of your .d.ts and fails CI when it changes without review. @arethetypeswrong/cli checks the package for module and types problems.
  • Type tests: tsd, expect-type, or vitest --typecheck assert that public types stay as intended (expectTypeOf(fn).returns.toEqualTypeOf<string>()).
  • State supported TypeScript versions. A new TS feature in your .d.ts can break users on older compilers. typesVersions can serve different declarations per TS version.
  • Do not export internal types. Everything exported becomes a promise.

B. HTTP APIs consumed by TS clients

  • Additive changes only within a version: new optional fields and new endpoints are fine; removing or renaming fields, changing types or meanings is breaking.
  • Tolerant readers: clients ignore unknown fields and handle unknown enum values ('unknown' fallback) instead of crashing.
  • Version breaking changes (/v2/... or a version header) and run both versions during the migration period.
  • Contract tests in CI: generated types from the OpenAPI spec, plus a diff tool (oasdiff) that flags breaking changes.
  • Mobile and cached web clients can run old code for months. Monitor usage of deprecated fields before removing them.

Follow-up: "Is adding a field to a response type breaking?" Answer: for the HTTP contract, no. For TypeScript, usually no, but it breaks code that constructs that type itself (test fixtures, mocks) or implements it, because the new field is now required there. Making it optional avoids this.

Q70

What trade-offs does TypeScript introduce?

Answer it out loud first. Then check.

Costs:

  1. Tooling and build complexity: compiler configuration, type-checking step in CI, source maps, module resolution settings (Q64), declaration files for libraries.
  2. Build and editor speed: type checking a large codebase takes time, and complex types slow down the editor. (Fast transpilers and the native compiler port reduce this.)
  3. Learning curve: generics, conditional and mapped types, variance. Advanced library types can be hard to read, and error messages can be long.
  4. Over-engineering risk: "type gymnastics" that nobody else on the team can maintain. Types become a second program to debug.
  5. False sense of security: types are erased (Q62). any, as and ! can lie. External data is unchecked unless you validate it. Unsound corners exist.
  6. Friction with JavaScript patterns and libraries: dynamic code, missing or wrong @types, version mismatches between a library and its types.
  7. Slower prototyping: for a throwaway script or a quick experiment, writing types can cost more than it saves.
  8. Hiring and onboarding: juniors from plain JavaScript need time to become productive with strict types.

Benefits:

  1. Bugs caught before runtime: null access, typos, wrong arguments, missing cases.
  2. Safe refactoring: rename a field or change a function signature, and the compiler lists every place to update.
  3. Editor support: autocomplete, go-to-definition, find references, inline documentation, automatic imports.
  4. Types as documentation that cannot go stale: a function signature tells you what it accepts and returns.
  5. Better design: discriminated unions and explicit contracts push you to model states and boundaries clearly.
  6. Team scale: large teams can change code they did not write with more confidence.

When the trade-off favors TypeScript: codebases with several developers, code that lives longer than a few months, libraries consumed by others, complex domains, frequent refactoring.

When plain JavaScript (maybe with JSDoc + // @ts-check) is reasonable: small scripts, quick prototypes, one-person tools, environments where a build step is not possible.

How to keep the costs low:

  • Prefer simple, readable types over clever ones. Inference for locals, explicit types at module boundaries.
  • Validate external data at runtime so the types tell the truth.
  • Use fast transpilation for development and run full type checks in CI and the editor.
  • Agree on team conventions (no any, limited as) and enforce them with lint rules.

The answer interviewers want: a balanced view. Candidates who only praise TypeScript sound like they have used it only on small projects. Name the costs, explain how you control them, then give your verdict: for team projects and anything long-lived, TypeScript is worth it.

Follow-up: "Have you ever found TypeScript getting in the way? What did you do?" Answer with a real example: a library with wrong types (you wrote a local declaration or wrapper), or an over-complex generic you simplified. Prepare one true story before the interview.
